candidateText:
Since revenue is actually up 15% while margin collapsed from 24% to 6%, the decline has to be driven by costs growing faster than revenue, so I'd weight my structure there — but I want to confirm the revenue side first so we don't miss a mix issue.

Three buckets:

First, revenue quality. Is the 15% growth coming from new store openings, same-store traffic, or price? Growth from new stores can carry heavy upfront costs and drag margin even if each store is healthy.

Second, costs — split fixed versus variable. Variable: coffee beans, dairy, cups, hourly labor. Fixed: rent, salaried staff, corporate overhead, marketing, any D&A from the expansion.

Third, external: commodity prices, wage legislation, competitive pricing pressure.

I'd start by asking which cost lines grew fastest in absolute dollars over the two years. Do we have a cost breakdown as a percent of revenue for both years?

Without competitor or elasticity data I'll assume specialty coffee has moderate pricing power, so price is part of the answer but not all 24 points. Other levers, roughly in order of impact:

Procurement. Beans are ~15 points of revenue. With 200 locations there's scale to consolidate suppliers, sign longer fixed-price contracts, or hedge green coffee futures — even a 10% reduction on beans is 1.5 points of margin back.

Waste and portioning. Dairy and food spoil. If yield loss is a few percent of that 43-point block, tightening it is a point or two with no customer impact.

Mix. Push higher-margin items — espresso drinks over food, where food carries dairy and spoilage. Same traffic, better basket margin.

Overhead, up 2 points, is the smallest lever but worth a look.

And price architecture rather than a blunt increase: raise sizes and add-ons, where customers anchor less.

candidateText:
My recommendation: Brew & Bean's margin problem is almost entirely an input-cost pass-through failure, and the fix is a staged price increase paired with procurement reform — not a cost-cutting program.

Three supports. First, COGS explains roughly 89% of the 18-point decline; labor is flat and overhead moved only 2 points. Second, within COGS, beans rose 40% and other inputs a similar amount — this is broad inflation, not one bad line. Third, menu prices haven't moved in two years while volume grew 15%, so the company absorbed all of it voluntarily. Demand is healthy; that's the asset to work with.

Specifically: phase in roughly 10–12% in price over two or three moves, weighted toward sizes and add-ons, and target the remaining gap through consolidated bean contracts and hedging, plus waste reduction.

Risks: I don't have elasticity or competitor pricing, so a 24% move at once could break traffic. Next steps — test price in a subset of stores, and pull category-level margins to target the increase.
